method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group) 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014' (June 2014), 21 claims; LICENCE: © American Academy of Ophthalmology; AAO terms bar reproduction or loading into AI programs without permission (read at page footer and https://www.aao.org/terms-of-service). S2: QUOTED from Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368) 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis' (published 29 September 2022), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9600940). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every S1 (AAO 2014) claim unchanged and adds S2, a CC BY 2022 narrative review (quoted), for PCR sampling, persistent and metaherpetic epithelial disease, stromal subtypes, trabeculitis and uveitis, steroid alternatives, neovascularisation and resistance. S2's drug tables (Tables 1-3) were stripped.

claims.claim: **Name the disease by the layer involved, because it sets the treatment:** epithelial (dendritic or geographic ulcer), stromal (with or without ulceration) or endothelial (formerly 'disciform'). Fluorescein shows whether a stromal keratitis is ulcerated, which decides the antiviral–steroid balance.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Epithelial disease is active viral infection and needs antivirals; stromal disease is mainly immune** and usually needs an antiviral plus a topical steroid.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A typical dendrite is a slit-lamp diagnosis;** laboratory tests are rarely needed and do not help in stromal disease, where virus usually cannot be grown. Keep testing for atypical cases.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Children get worse disease:** more often bilateral, combined epithelial and stromal, recurring within the first year, and misdiagnosed. Scarring can cause amblyopia, so watch them more closely than adults. (Strong, moderate quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask about atopy** in severe, bilateral or treatment-resistant disease; bilateral cases are often misdiagnosed, and atopic patients tend to respond better to oral than topical antivirals. (Strong, moderate quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Steroids by any route (drops, intravitreal or systemic) can provoke severe epithelial keratitis,** and prostaglandin-analogue glaucoma drops are best avoided in patients with a history of HSV.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Any eye surgery in a patient with past ocular HSV:** strongly consider antiviral cover around the operation, particularly while steroid drops are in use.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat with an antiviral alone, and keep topical steroids out of the initial management.** (Strong, good quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Oral aciclovir 400 mg five times daily did at least as well as topical aciclovir ointment five times daily** in two randomised trials. Topical aciclovir is not an FDA-approved eye product but is widely used outside the US.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Two antivirals at once do not speed healing, and debridement alone is not adequate treatment** (use it only if antivirals are contraindicated or unavailable).
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Use oral antivirals cautiously over age 65 and in renal impairment,** as all three can be nephrotoxic; reduce doses and lengthen intervals in renal insufficiency, planned with a nephrologist.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For an atypical lesion, PCR is the most sensitive test,** far better than viral culture, but sample before starting antivirals; vital dyes can interfere with PCR.
claims.source_text: For less typical presentations that are not as readily identifiable on clinical presentation, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) has been used to confirm the diagnosis of epithelial HSK. Additional, more recent methods include tear collection to determine viral load and immunofluorescence antibody assay (IFA) to detect the viral antigen. PCR is the most sensitive method, and far superior to viral culture. However, this must be utilized prior to initiating antiviral treatment for best accuracy. It has been reported that using vital dyes may also interfere with PCR accuracy and inhibit HSV DNA detection
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **US topical antivirals:** trifluridine is given up to nine times a day and can be toxic to the epithelium; ganciclovir gel is given five times a day with less toxicity; they appear similarly effective.
claims.source_text: Trifluridine is a topical antiviral that is a pyrimidine nucleoside, used for epithelial keratitis. The frequency of administration limits its use, as it is prescribed up to nine times per day and may thus lead to epithelial toxicity. On the other hand, ganciclovir gel, a purine nucleoside, is dosed less at five times per day, with less propensity for epithelial toxicity. Both topical forms of antivirals appear to be comparable in efficacy, despite their differences
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Persistent epithelial disease** is usually poor adherence to the antiviral, rarely resistance, or metaherpetic (neurotrophic) ulceration without active virus. Treat metaherpetic disease with lubricants, temporary tarsorrhaphy, therapeutic ptosis, amniotic membrane, autologous serum or recombinant human nerve growth factor.
claims.source_text: Persistent epithelial keratitis is often due to poor compliance with antiviral administration or, rarely, from antiviral resistance. Another consideration for persistence is metaherpetic keratitis, following ulceration in the absence of active viral infection. The reason for this is neurotrophic in nature and can be managed by the use of topical lubricants, temporary tarsorrhaphy, therapeutic ptosis, amniotic membrane, topical autologous serum, or recombinant human nerve growth factor
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat with a topical steroid plus an oral antiviral for at least ten weeks,** adjusting the balance according to whether the epithelium is ulcerated. (Strong, good quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Why longer than ten weeks:** in HEDS a ten-week prednisolone taper cut treatment failure to 26% from 73% on placebo, but half the steroid group failed within six weeks of stopping. The steroid taper should therefore run beyond ten weeks, titrated to response.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prefer oral over topical antivirals here:** the US topical agents penetrate the stroma poorly, and long-term trifluridine is toxic to the ocular surface.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Stromal keratitis with epithelial ulceration is the form most often mistaken for microbial keratitis.** It is under-studied; the evidence favours therapeutic-dose oral antiviral with careful topical steroid.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stromal keratitis (20–48% of ocular HSV) is necrotising or, more often, non-necrotising (disciform) immune keratitis.** The necrotising form risks corneal melt; repeated attacks bring scarring, new vessels, thinning and lipid deposition.
claims.source_text: Once the virus invades the stroma, it is deemed a stromal keratitis, which accounts for 20-48% of all ocular HSV infections … The stromal forms of HSV keratitis can be classified as necrotizing and non-necrotizing, or disciform, keratitis. The necrotizing form of stromal keratitis appears as a fulminant stromal invasion of the virus, with or without epithelial ulceration. Due to the severity of the inflammatory response to the virus, patients who suffer from this form of stromal keratitis are at risk of corneal melt. The more common form is the non-necrotizing immune stromal keratitis. This is distinguished from the other form in that there is no necrosis, despite the presence of stromal inflammation, and a less likelihood of epithelial compromise. Clinically, this may manifest as a disciform lesion or ring, representing the deposition of the immune complex within the stroma. Edema is also commonly present in the inferior region of the corneal stroma, with or without the presence of keratic precipitates. Chronicity and recurrence of stromal disease leads to scarring, neovascularization, corneal thinning, and lipid deposition.
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Topical steroid is first line for the inflammation of stromal keratitis, endotheliitis, trabeculitis and uveitis.** In HEDS it cut inflammation by 68% against placebo, yet final vision was the same, so delaying or forgoing it did not cost vision.
claims.source_text: To dampen the significant inflammatory effects of HSV, particularly in stromal keratitis, endotheliitis, trabeculitis, and uveitis, topical corticosteroids are the first line treatment. … The ultimate endpoint visual acuity between the antiviral and placebo group versus antiviral plus corticosteroids was the same. As such, delaying or forgoing the use of corticosteroids does not bear any additional visual detriment. HEDS ultimately concluded that the use of topical corticosteroids reduced inflammation by 68% as compared to placebo
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Topical ciclosporin is an option in non-necrotising disease or when steroid works poorly,** given steroid-related raised pressure and cataract.
claims.source_text: Because of the known adverse effects of corticosteroids, particularly raised intraocular pressure and cataract, alternative treatments such as topical cyclosporine have offered some benefit in non-necrotizing infections [,]. Topical cyclosporine may be helpful for patients who respond poorly to corticosteroids.
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Map new vessels with fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography,** since the slit lamp alone underestimates them. Angiography-guided fine-needle diathermy of feeder vessels works well when few are present, usually in three or fewer sessions; anti-VEGF results are variable.
claims.source_text: In order to accurately assess the degree and presence of neovascularization, multimodal imaging utilizing fluorescein and indocyanine green is superior to slit lamp examination alone, as this may underestimate the degree of the condition. Specific interventions include angiography guided fine needle diathermy of afferent feeder vessels, which is highly effective in cases where few feeder vessels are readily identified. This treatment is repeatable, with patients usually requiring approximately three or less sessions in total … For multiple feeder vessels that are not as readily localized, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) has been attempted with varying results. Its efficacy for corneal disease, especially neovascularization, which is already present, is questionable
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Treat with a topical steroid plus an oral antiviral.** (Strong, good quality) Mean healing in trials took 21 to 25 days, faster than stromal disease, so prolonged treatment may not be needed.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **HSV endotheliitis or uveitis often raises intraocular pressure** and may cause iris atrophy. For stromal keratitis with trabeculitis or uveitis, combine topical and oral antivirals with topical steroid; oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily is needed to reach the anterior chamber.
claims.source_text: HSV can penetrate further into the anterior segment, leading to endotheliitis and uveitis that is unique in that it often raises intraocular pressure and may present with iris atrophy … Stromal keratitis with trabeculitis and/or uveitis is complex in management, often necessitating the use of topical and oral antivirals, as well as topical corticosteroids. In order to penetrate the anterior chamber, acyclovir at a dose of 800 mg five times daily is warranted, in addition to the normal topical therapeutic dose
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Recurrent stromal keratitis: give long-term (one year or more) low-dose oral prophylaxis** — aciclovir 400 mg twice daily or valaciclovir 500 mg once daily, the only regimens proven to cut recurrence; famciclovir 250 mg twice daily is a reasonable alternative. (Strong, good quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In HEDS, a year of prophylaxis roughly halved recurrences, with no lasting effect once it stopped;** the benefit was greatest after stromal keratitis or multiple recurrences.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **After penetrating keratoplasty for HSV: oral aciclovir 800 mg three times a day, later reduced to 400 mg twice a day; keep it going a year or longer,** and for as long as topical steroid continues. (Strong, good quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect resistance with frequent recurrence despite prophylaxis, or treatment failure in an immunocompromised patient,** and consider susceptibility testing: aciclovir resistance reaches 6.4% in immunocompetent patients. (Strong, moderate quality)
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recurrence is common:** 40% of patients have 2–5 relapses and 11% have 6–15. Stromal involvement brings more recurrence and the greatest threat to vision.
claims.source_text: As such, recurrence is common; 40% of patients experience 2-5 relapses and 11% experience 6-15 relapses … Once it invades the corneal stroma, it results in a more severe visual compromise and risk of recurrence
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Aciclovir resistance comes from HSV thymidine kinase mutations,** and prolonged prophylaxis carries a resistance risk. Foscarnet, which does not depend on viral thymidine kinase, is often used for resistant infection.
claims.source_text: Since it is phosphorylated by HSV thymidine kinase, mutations in thymidine kinase can lead to acyclovir resistance. … Caution should be exercised due to risk of developing antiviral resistance with prolonged use … Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analogue DNA polymerase inhibitor. Because of its mechanism of action, it is often used in cases of acyclovir resistance because it is not metabolized by viral thymidine kinase.
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Valaciclovir, a prodrug of aciclovir, has 3–5 times its bioavailability,** comparable to intravenous dosing; famciclovir is the least used of the three oral agents.
claims.source_text: Valaciclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir but has a greater bioavailability that is 3-5 times greater than acyclovir and comparable to intravenous forms. Famciclovir is a guanosine analog and is the least commonly used of the three
claims.locator: Labib BA, Chigbu DI, Diagnostics 12(10):2368 (doi 10.3390/diagnostics12102368), 'Clinical Management of Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis', published 29 September 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9600940/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Diagnosis and management belong with an ophthalmologist** because of the risk of blindness; teach patients the warning signs of recurrence and the need to return promptly.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology clinical statement (White ML, Chodosh J; endorsed by the Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group), 'Herpes Simplex Virus Keratitis: A Treatment Guideline - 2014', June 2014, https://www.aao.org/education/clinical-statement/herpes-simplex-virus-keratitis-treatment-guideline, retrieved 2026-09-23
